title: Dirty Pretty Things
full_review:
A Nigerian immigrant working as the night clerk in a London hotel stumbles upon a black market trade in body organs in the melancholy "Dirty Pretty Things" (Miramax).
Director Stephen Frears makes visible in this movie the illegal immigrants in minimum-wage jobs that society ignores or takes for granted. And Steven Knight's well-crafted script builds suspense alongside character development.

An international cast of actors also lends credibility to this tale of the displaced and dispossessed.

A physician before having to flee his native land, illegal immigrant Okwe (Chiwetel Ejiofor) drives a cab by day and is a hotel desk clerk by night. He catches a few hours' shut-eye by renting the couch of hotel maid Senay (Audrey Tautou), a virginal Turk seeking asylum, who can be deported if the immigration bureaucrats discover she is working.

One night at the small hotel, Okwe gets a complaint about a clogged toilet and to his horror finds the culprit is a human heart. The Spanish manager, Sneaky (Sergei Lopez), threatens to expose Okwe if he calls the police. The manager has been orchestrating a highly profitable kidneys-for-passports black market operation and when he finds out Okwe is a doctor tries to force him to no avail to perform the risky surgeries.

Meanwhile, to elude suspicious immigration officers, Senay has quit the hotel for a sweatshop where the piggish supervisor blackmails her into granting sexual favors. Okwe's Chinese friend (Benedict Wong), a hospital morgue attendant, gives her shelter in the morbid surroundings since her apartment is being watched by the authorities, but she decides she must accept Sneaky's offer of a passport for her kidney. Okwe steps in with an alternative which would seem to give Sneaky just what he wanted: a skilled surgeon and a healthy, willing patient. But sneaky is an adjective better applied to the resourceful Nigerian.
Okwe's mysterious background and the possibility of romance with Senay add another element to this soulful story whose only problematic area is when a friendly hotel prostitute (Sophie Okonedo) advises Senay about the abortion pill.

Strong performances certainly add to the sleek allure of this strange blend of film noir with a little twist of black comedy. But it is just as much a rather heartbreaking look at abused aliens with little recourse but disturbingly desperate measures.
Because of its theme of sexual exploitation, abortion reference, surgical gore, fleeting drug abuse, frequent rough language and minimal profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
